clues.q: This Barbadian singer topped charts in 2007 with “Umbrella.”
This British singer of “Rolling in the Deep” and “Hello” named albums after her age, such as “21” and “25.”
Which instrument is Yo-Yo Ma famous for playing?
This Cuban-born singer, called the “Queen of Salsa,” was famous for her catchphrase “¡Azúcar!”
This Indian sitar virtuoso taught George Harrison and was the father of singer Norah Jones.
In this 1994 film, Tom Hanks’s title character recalls that his mama always said life was like a box of chocolates.
This animated family from Springfield, including Bart and Lisa, got its own Fox series in 1989.
In this 1999 sci-fi film, Keanu Reeves plays Neo, who takes the red pill.
This 2001 French film stars Audrey Tautou as a shy, imaginative waitress in Montmartre, Paris.
This 2022 Telugu-language film’s song “Naatu Naatu” won the Academy Award for Best Original Song.
By tradition first held in 776 BCE, this ancient Greek athletic festival took place every four years in the western Peloponnese.
clues.a: What are the Olympic Games (the Olympics)?

clues.q: In 1922, Howard Carter discovered this boy pharaoh’s nearly intact tomb in the Valley of the Kings.
This Athenian philosopher, teacher of Plato, was sentenced to death by drinking hemlock in 399 BCE.
This Mesoamerican people built the cities of Tikal and Palenque and developed a sophisticated calendar.
In 49 BCE, Julius Caesar led his army across this small river, starting a civil war; crossing it now means passing a point of no return.
In 2004, Mark Zuckerberg launched this social network from his Harvard dorm room.
This August 1969 music festival on a farm in Bethel, New York, featured Jimi Hendrix and Janis Joplin.
Opened in 1994, this undersea rail link connects Folkestone, England, with Coquelles, near Calais.
On October 3, 1990, the eastern and western parts of this European country were reunified.
First launched in 1981, this NASA program of reusable orbiters flew 135 missions before retiring in 2011.
This boy who refuses to grow up leads the Lost Boys in Neverland.
This Russian author wrote the epic novels “War and Peace” and “Anna Karenina.”
George Orwell’s 1949 dystopian novel warns that “Big Brother is watching you.”
Gabriel García Márquez’s 1967 novel chronicles generations of the Buendía family in the town of Macondo.
clues.a: What is One Hundred Years of Solitude?

clues.q: Murasaki Shikibu, a lady-in-waiting at the Japanese imperial court, wrote this classic early-11th-century story of a shining prince.
clues.a: What is The Tale of Genji?

clues.q: In Greek myth, this king of the gods ruled from Mount Olympus and hurled thunderbolts.
This Norse god of thunder wields the hammer Mjölnir.
Dipped in the River Styx as a baby, this Greek hero was vulnerable only at his heel.
This jackal-headed Egyptian god was associated with mummification and the afterlife.
In Norse myth, this immense ash tree links the nine worlds.

questions.q: Huge desert covering much of North Africa?
Who painted the Sistine Chapel ceiling?

clues.q: This Minneapolis musician released the album and film “Purple Rain” in 1984.
clues.hint: His name, given at birth, is also a royal title.

clues.q: Fronted by Bono, this Irish band released “The Joshua Tree” in 1987.
clues.hint: Its name is one letter and one digit.

clues.q: Known as the “Waltz King,” which composer wrote “The Blue Danube”?
clues.hint: His father, a composer too, had the same name.

clues.q: This Nigerian bandleader and activist is celebrated as a pioneer of Afrobeat in the 1970s.
clues.hint: His Lagos nightclub was called the Afrika Shrine.

clues.q: This French composer wrote the piano piece “Clair de lune” and the orchestral work “La Mer.”
clues.hint: Often called a leading figure of musical Impressionism.

clues.q: Steven Spielberg’s 1975 thriller follows a great white shark menacing the beaches of Amity Island.
clues.hint: Its two-note theme was composed by John Williams.

clues.q: In this 2003 Pixar film, a clownfish named Marlin crosses the ocean to find his missing son.
clues.hint: Dory, a forgetful blue tang, helps out.

clues.q: This NBC sitcom about six pals in Manhattan who hang out at the Central Perk coffeehouse ran from 1994 to 2004.
clues.hint: Rachel, Ross, Monica, Chandler, Joey and Phoebe.

clues.q: In Federico Fellini’s 1960 film, Anita Ekberg wades into Rome’s Trevi Fountain.
clues.hint: A photographer character gave us the word “paparazzi.”

clues.q: This 2016 Barry Jenkins film won Best Picture after a famous envelope mix-up in which “La La Land” was first announced.
clues.hint: Its three chapters follow a character named Chiron.

clues.q: Romans built these structures, often carried on tall arches, to bring water into their cities.
clues.hint: France’s Pont du Gard is a famous example.

clues.q: This Greek writer from Halicarnassus is often called the “Father of History.”
clues.hint: His “Histories” describe the wars between Greeks and Persians.

clues.q: This female pharaoh of Egypt’s 18th Dynasty built a grand mortuary temple at Deir el-Bahari.
clues.hint: She was often shown wearing a ceremonial false beard.

clues.q: Carved into rose-red cliffs by the Nabataeans, this ancient city lies in southern Jordan.
clues.hint: Its Treasury facade appears in “Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade.”

clues.q: This ancient kingdom in what is now Ethiopia and Eritrea is famous for its towering carved stone stelae.
clues.hint: Its capital, a city in northern Ethiopia, shares its name.

clues.q: Larry Page and Sergey Brin founded this company in 1998.
clues.hint: Its name plays on a 1 followed by 100 zeros.

clues.q: In 1986, this famous comet returned to the inner solar system, as it does roughly every 76 years.
clues.hint: Named for an English astronomer, Edmond, who predicted its return.

clues.q: In 1999, Portugal handed over this territory on China’s southern coast to Chinese sovereignty.
clues.hint: Famous for casinos and the Ruins of St. Paul’s.

clues.q: Launched by NASA in 1977, these twin space probes each carry a gold-plated record of sounds and images from Earth.
clues.a: What are the Voyager probes (Voyager 1 and 2)?
clues.hint: Both flew past Jupiter and Saturn.

clues.q: In 1960, this politician of Ceylon, now Sri Lanka, became the world’s first female prime minister.
clues.hint: She succeeded her late husband as party leader.

clues.q: This capital on the Seine is home to the Louvre museum.
clues.hint: Nicknamed the “City of Light.”

clues.q: In 1960, Brazil moved its capital to Brasília from this coastal city.
clues.hint: Home of Copacabana beach.

clues.q: Home to Hoàn Kiếm Lake, this city on the Red River is Vietnam’s capital.
clues.hint: It is not Ho Chi Minh City.

clues.q: This capital of Ecuador sits high in the Andes, just south of the equator.
clues.hint: Its old town was among the first UNESCO World Heritage Sites.

clues.q: Kazakhstan’s capital, this city was officially called Nur-Sultan from 2019 to 2022.
clues.hint: Home to the Bayterek observation tower.

clues.q: This German-born physicist developed the special and general theories of relativity.
clues.hint: Famous for E = mc².

clues.q: This Polish-born scientist was the first person to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences.
clues.hint: She discovered polonium and radium with her husband.

clues.q: This English naturalist sailed on HMS Beagle and published “On the Origin of Species” in 1859.
clues.hint: Think Galápagos finches.

clues.q: This 19th-century friar’s experiments with pea plants laid the foundations of genetics.
clues.hint: He worked at an abbey in Brno.

clues.q: Working in Cairo, this Arab scholar wrote the influential 11th-century “Book of Optics.”
clues.hint: He was born in Basra around 965.

questions.q: How many bones are in a typical adult human body?
Which planet spins tipped on its side, with an axis tilted about 98 degrees?
In which country is the historic city of Timbuktu?
What color do you get by mixing blue and yellow paint?
What is the capital of Spain?

rounds.name: Final Round
rounds.q: In the mid-1400s, this goldsmith from Mainz, Germany, developed a movable-type printing press that transformed the spread of books in Europe.
rounds.hint: A famous printed Bible bears his name.
